name: MemSearcher

paper.title: MemSearcher: Training LLMs to Reason, Search and Manage Memory via End-to-End Reinforcement Learning

construction.unit: one natural-language memory passage per question
construction.kept_as: LLM rewrite of the previous memory plus the new search results
construction.processing: after each search, the same LLM reads question, memory, its thought, the call and the passages, and writes a new memory

organization.stores: one memory string, overwritten every turn

management.operations: overwrite the whole memory each turn (keep relevant details, add new ones)
management.forgetting: thoughts, calls and passages leave the context after each turn; only what the model writes into memory survives

retrieval.candidates: none: the whole memory is in every turn's prompt (the search tool retrieves Wikipedia passages, not memory)
retrieval.budget: memory up to 1,024 tokens (paper); each memory write is capped at 512 new tokens in the code

use.context: system prompt + question + memory; no earlier turns
use.reasoning: multi-turn: think, then answer in \boxed{} or search; one memory update per search

classify.note: A single rewritten memory string replaces the growing ReAct history; what to keep is learned by RL, and the memory is always read whole.

stages.ingestion: Each turn the search tool returns Wikipedia passages (2018 dump, E5 retriever) for the model's query.
stages.construction: In a second generation call the same LLM reads the question, previous memory, its thought, the call and the passages, and writes an updated memory inside <memory> tags.
stages.organization: One plain-text memory; no structure or index.
stages.update: The new memory overwrites the old one; the prompt asks to keep relevant earlier details and add new ones. The paper caps memory at 1,024 tokens; in training a trajectory ends if the cap is exceeded.
stages.retrieval: None for memory: the next turn's prompt is the system prompt, the question and the whole memory.
stages.answer: When the memory suffices, the model answers in \boxed{}; otherwise it searches again, up to the turn limit.
stages.learning: Multi-context GRPO: each trajectory's reward (format check plus answer F1) gives one group-normalised advantage that is copied to every turn, and each turn is optimised as a separate sample. Trained on NQ + HotpotQA, 5 rollouts per question.

summary: A search agent that keeps a compact, LLM-rewritten memory instead of the growing ReAct history, so each turn sees only the question and the memory; the policy learns what to keep through multi-context GRPO.
notes: Venue checked on the ACL Anthology: Findings of ACL 2026, 2026.findings-acl.736, under the title 'MemSearcher: Iterative Memory Integration for Search Agent via End-to-End Reinforcement Learning'. The arXiv comment says 'Accepted to ACL 2026', but the proceedings list it in Findings. Main-table numbers in the Anthology PDF match arXiv v2 (8 May 2026), which was read in full. Memory is per question (a working buffer), not kept across questions.

headline: Each turn the model sees only the question and one memory it wrote itself; all earlier thoughts and passages are gone.
The memory is rewritten, not appended: facts can enter from the model's own knowledge (the paper's case study stores a fact the passage does not contain).
Retrieval here is Wikipedia search; the memory itself is never searched.

discussion.takeaway: Replacing the growing ReAct history with one memory the model rewrites every turn keeps the context small and, after RL training, gives higher EM than ReAct-style search agents of the same or larger size.

claims.claim: MemSearcher beats search-agent baselines at every size.
Smaller MemSearcher models beat larger baselines.
Context stays nearly constant across turns.
claims.evidence: Under 4K tokens vs a linear rise for ReSearch (Fig. 4, §4.2.2).

claims.claim: RL is needed, and beats SFT.
claims.evidence: 3B: 14.4 without RL, 28.5 with SFT, 43.8 with RL (Tables 3-4).

claims.claim: A middle memory size is best.
claims.evidence: 256 to 2,048 tokens; gains up to 1,024 on Musique, saturated at 256 on Bamboogle (Fig. 6, §4.3.3).

limits: Only a simple memory design is studied; RAG-like or structured memories for RL search agents are left open.
Multi-context GRPO may carry length bias, and more RL techniques remain to be explored.
reading: The memory is per question and lives for at most a handful of turns; it is context compression for multi-hop QA, not long-term memory.
Caps of 1,024 and 2,048 give the same scores on all eight curves of Fig. 6, which fits the code writing each memory with at most 512 new tokens.

Baselines are listed with sizes but no statement of who ran them or with which retriever; the paper notes ZeroSearch and R1-Searcher used Google search in their own evaluation, so those rows at least are not under the same retrieval setup.
The case study (Table 6) writes 'Sylvester comes from Latin' into memory after a passage about a singer, so the rewrite can add unsourced facts.
Table 3's 'without training' baseline is the untrained model inside the MemSearcher loop, not a ReAct agent, so it measures RL rather than memory.

abstract.text: Search agents in the ReAct style append every thought, call and retrieved passage to their context, which grows long and noisy. MemSearcher instead keeps one compact memory: each turn the model sees the question and the memory, searches, and then rewrites the memory from the new passages, so context length stays nearly flat. Because each turn has its own context, the authors train it with multi-context GRPO, which gives every turn the trajectory's advantage. On seven QA datasets MemSearcher models from 3B to 14B beat RL-trained ReAct-style search agents while keeping contexts under 4K tokens.
